sections.html: The tiger lotus (Nymphaea zenkeri) is a bulb plant with broad, wavy-edged leaves and a variegated colour pattern. It has two kinds of leaves: completely submersed, somewhat heart-shaped leaves that grow near the bulb, and floating leaves on long, thin stems that look like lily pads resting at the surface. Some tiger lotuses grow primarily green leaves with red variegation, whereas others have red leaves with darker, reddish-purple striping.

• Common name: Red tiger lotus
  • Scientific name: Nymphaea zenkeri
  • Lighting: Medium to high
  • Substrate: needed
  • Growth rate: fast
  • Placement: mid-ground or background
  • Height: 15–60+ cm
  • Fertilizers: not needed to low
  • CO2: not needed to low
  • Propagation: daughter plants via bulbs or seeds
Red tiger lotus (Nymphaea zenkeri) is a flowering plant of the Nymphaeaceae family, native to Southeast Asia and tropical West Africa. It is also known as tiger lotus or Nymphaea lotus.

Red tiger lotus is found in ditches of stagnant water, along the edges of lakes and ponds, and in other areas of stagnant water. The relatively shallow water of its native habitat has made the plant quite tolerant of water temperature, lighting and dissolved CO2.

• Sen tiger lớn lên khá to, trồng ở trung cảnh hoặc hậu cảnh là vừa.
  • Lấy củ ra khỏi chậu nhựa, gỡ hết bông đá rồi rửa sạch cặn bám.
  • Ấn nhẹ khoảng một phần ba củ xuống nền, chồi và lá phải nằm hẳn bên trên. Đừng vùi cả củ, vì vùi hết thì củ sẽ thối.
  • Củ mới thả có thể bị nổi. Cứ chờ nó ngấm đủ nước thì nó sẽ chìm, rồi rễ ăn xuống nền sẽ giữ củ đứng chắc. Mấy lá non nhú từ củ thường dập khi vận chuyển, hoặc có thể tan sau khi trồng. Củ còn khỏe mới là phần quan trọng nhất.

Planting: the bulb arrives in a plastic pot covered in rock wool. Small leaves sprouting from the bulb are often damaged in transit or may melt away after planting, but a healthy bulb is the most important part. Remove the bulb from the pot and rock wool, and rinse off any debris. Tiger lotuses get rather large, so plant it in the midground or background. Gently push one-third of the bulb into the substrate so that the shoots or leaves are completely above ground. Do not bury the entire bulb or it will rot. If the bulb floats at first, wait for it to become waterlogged enough to sink. As the roots grow into the substrate, they will firmly anchor the bulb.

Growing: once well established, it quickly grows plenty of big leaves, so feed it with comprehensive fertilisers such as Easy Green and Easy Root Tabs. To bring out the red colour, provide medium to high lighting with some extra iron fertiliser.

Pruning: the plant may grow so many floating leaves that it blocks light from other plants. To trim, clip the lily pad at the base of its stem, closest to the bulb. Continuously pruning a few floating leaves keeps the plant from growing too tall and makes it grow bushier.

The tiger lotus can grow flowers at the surface. If it has lots of lily pads, it may produce a flower with colours ranging from white to yellow. When the flower wilts, it may develop into multiple seeds that can be collected. Another method is via the bulb: if the plant is doing well, the parent bulb may form small daughter bulbs that can be detached and replanted in another aquarium.

Sometimes bulb plants have a dormant period, where all the leaves die off and leave just the bulb. One option is to keep the bulb in the tank; after several months it will start sprouting new leaves. You can also take the bulb out, keep it in a damp container for several months, and then put it back into the tank, after which new leaves will sprout and begin growing again.

Red tiger lotus has arrow-shaped or heart-shaped red leaves, which can develop striped variegation under intense lighting. It sends lily pads to the water surface and produces blue or white flowers. When the flowers wilt, the fruit bears seeds, which serve to propagate the plant. The seeds develop into bulbs that root in the substrate and a new plant begins to grow. Blossoms are usually white, but through selective breeding and hybridisation there are varieties with blue or red flowers.

The height ranges from 15 to 60+ cm and it can grow taller under optimal conditions. Growth is fast, and the strong root system can spread all over the tank if not contained.

Tank size

The plant thrives in a variety of tank sizes, even nano tanks if properly maintained, but the recommended minimum is 40 litres.

Water

Temperature 22–28°C. Lower temperatures often result in dormancy and deterioration. pH 6.0–8.0 is optimal. The plant tolerates soft or hard water but appreciates 2–15 dGH.

Lighting

It is not demanding and can grow even in low light, but medium to high light is recommended because the plant grows more compact and dense under it.

Substrate

It does well in a well-fertilized, nutrient-rich substrate. Many aquarists believe an iron-rich clay gravel substrate is ideal for its nutrient needs and abundant root system. Any nutrient-rich substrate (such as ADA Amazonia, Caribsea Eco-Complete, Seachem Flourite Black Sand) is a good choice.

CO2 and fertilizer

It can do without CO2 and additional nutrients. Low CO2 injection, root tabs or liquid fertilizers can give more vibrant, lush plants, but do not oversupply if you do not want very large plants. If you keep shrimp with it, note that high CO2 levels and copper (present in most fertilizers) are extremely dangerous to shrimp.

Planting and propagation

The plant is sold as bulbs with or without leaves. Bulbs must not be completely buried, to prevent rot: place firm, healthy bulbs on the substrate surface and bury about half. If you cannot tell which side is the top, let the bulb float until new shoots grow, which can take from a few days to several months. A thick root system develops under the substrate. It appreciates a deep (at least 5 cm), well-fertilized substrate.

  • Rare in aquariums: propagation by seeds produced after the flowers wilt.
  • Common in aquariums: separating the bulb from the plant once the bulb or shoots have developed their own roots, then replanting.

Red tiger lotus should not be planted near sensitive plants, because it absorbs large amounts of nitrate, iron, CO2 and macro- and micronutrients, which can starve nearby plants.

Containing the root system

The root system can be very large. Containing the bulb prevents the roots from taking over the substrate. You need a plastic container holding at least four cups, fine nylon mesh fabric big enough to wrap it, a rubber band or fishing line, four cups of enriched substrate and root tab fertilizer.

  1. Fill the container with the substrate and root tab fertilizer.
  2. Wrap the container tightly with the fine mesh fabric.
  3. Cut a piece of fishing line about 20 cm long to tie the fabric.
  4. Gather the fabric together and twist it. Double the excess over itself and tie with the rubber band or fishing line.
  5. Place the container in the aquarium. It can be hidden with large flat rocks and pieces of wood.

The plant grows through the mesh while its roots stay in the container. Mesh makes it easier to add root tabs. With this method the plant will eventually consume everything in the container, so root tabs will need to be added later.

Maintenance and care

  • The plant grows very fast and can take over the tank if left unattended. Trim it from time to time.
  • To keep it bushy and dense, trim regularly to prevent it growing too tall. Cut leaves as close to the base as possible, as it is otherwise prone to rot.
  • To prevent seeds, cut surface leaves and flowers before they wilt and turn into fruit.
  • Rapid growth is fuelled by substrate nutrients, CO2 and lighting (medium to high). Limiting these factors, along with pruning and confining the bulb and roots, slows growth.

If allowed to form lily pads, the plant will flower. Experienced aquarists advise training the plant to grow underwater from the start: cut the pads off at the base to make it bushier, so it does not spend energy reaching the surface.

Benefits

  • Aquascape: a good choice for aquascapes (particularly Dutch style) and as a focal point.
  • Prevents gas pockets: the roots help break up anaerobic pockets in the substrate, including hydrogen sulfide (H2S), which can be dangerous to fish and shrimp.
  • Foraging place: an additional place for biofilm to grow, an ideal first food for newly hatched fry and baby shrimp.
  • Shelter: provides hiding places for shy fish and shrimp.
  • Oxygenation: like all plants, it oxygenates the water.

Problems

  • Outgrowth: it can grow very large and fast with plenty of light, CO2 and nutrients. Keep these balanced and trim leaves regularly.
  • Losing leaves: in low temperatures it can go dormant and shed all its leaves. It will produce new leaves after a while; give it a month or two. It is a seasonal plant and tends to die back before the larger leaves grow.
  • Relocation: the root system can be enormous. To remove the plant, cut it off rather than pulling it up, or you will pull everything up.
  • Burn marks: high light speeds up growth but can burn lily pads if the light hangs low and the plant reaches the surface.
  • Blocking light: the plant keeps sending out runners to the surface, then produces big leaves, taking advantage of atmospheric CO2. Remove lily pads now and then, as they block light for other plants.
  • Suppressing other plants: there is a rumour that it produces a chemical that suppresses algae and slows other plants. This is unconfirmed; the problem more likely lies in its huge root system and greed for nutrients, as it outcompetes and can strangle other rooted plants. Contain the root system and add root tabs for other plants.

Tankmates

It is compatible with fish (guppies, mollies, swordtails, angelfish, loaches, discus, platies, tetras, zebra danios, otocinclus), all shrimp (Neocaridina, Caridina, Amano, ghost, bamboo, vampire shrimp) and snails (ramshorn, nerite, Malaysian trumpet, Japanese trapdoor, mystery snails), though be careful with snails that eat plants. Avoid aggressive fish that tear up plants, such as Oscars, Frontosa, Texas cichlids, Red Devils and Jack Dempseys. Do not keep it with crayfish or crabs, which eat, cut and uproot plants. Compatible plants include Anubias, Anacharis, Java fern and water wisteria, ideally ones that do not compete for substrate nutrients and are not planted too close.

Buying

It is widely available and inexpensive, sold as bulbs with or without leaves, or as juvenile plants with roots and leaves. Good bulbs are firm and healthy-looking, not soft and squishy; roots and leaves should be abundant, fresh and undamaged. A plant with leaves but no bulb is fine if roots and leaves look healthy, and will form a new bulb later. The bulb is only food storage during dormancy.

Quarantine

Unless the plant was grown in vitro and the pot is intact, quarantine it before adding it to the aquarium. It can carry parasites, pests such as snails, or predators (dragonfly and damselfly nymphs), or may have been treated with pesticides that are extremely poisonous to fish, shrimp and other invertebrates.
